title: Acute Hepatitis and Acute Liver Failure

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: What is the most common clinical outcome of acute hepatitis?
questions.exp: Under acute hepatitis outcomes, recovery is explicitly annotated with '(m/c)', followed by chronic hepatitis and rare fulminant failure. (Book p993)

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: Match each demographic group with the most common viral cause of acute hepatitis — 1) Children 2) Adults … A) Hepatitis E virus (HEV) B) Hepatitis A virus (HAV)
questions.exp: Under viral causes of acute hepatitis, HAV is noted as '(m/c in children)' and HEV as '(m/c in adults)'. (Book p993)

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: Which of the following toxins is NOT listed under acute hepatitis causes on this page?
questions.exp: The toxins listed are Rat poison (Yellow Phosphorus), Mushroom, and Alcohol; carbon tetrachloride is not among them. (Book p993)

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: Which two pharmaceutical classes are highlighted under the drug causes of acute hepatitis on this page?
questions.exp: Under drug causes, the page lists Paracetamol and ATT (Anti-tubercular therapy). (Book p993)

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: Match each hepatitis virus with its taxonomic family and physical property — 1) Hepatitis A virus (HAV) 2) Hepatitis E virus (HEV) … A) Calicivirus family (Hepeviridae) with 4 genotypes B) Picornaviridae family; single-stranded RNA virus that is heat sensitive (>85°C)
questions.exp: HAV belongs to Picornaviridae, is ssRNA and heat sensitive (>85°C); HEV belongs to the Calicivirus-like Hepeviridae family and has 4 genotypes. (Book p993)

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: What are the average incubation periods of Hepatitis A virus (HAV) and Hepatitis E virus (HEV)?
questions.exp: In the comparison table, the incubation period is 30 days for HAV and 40 days for HEV. (Book p993)

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: Match each virus with its primary mechanism of hepatocellular injury — 1) Hepatitis A virus 2) Hepatitis E virus … A) Immune-mediated damage B) Direct cytopathic effect
questions.exp: The table specifies the injury mechanism as 'Cytopathic effect' for HAV and 'Immune mediated' for HEV. (Book p993)

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: Assess the two statements comparing HAV and HEV: I Cholestatic hepatitis with prominent pruritus is rare in HAV but marked (+++) in HEV. II Hepatitis A frequently progresses to chronic carrier status in adults.
questions.exp: Statement I is true because cholestatic hepatitis is rare in HAV and marked in HEV. Statement II is false because progression to chronicity is 'Not seen' in HAV. (Book p993)

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with a 3-day prodrome of low-grade fever, nausea, and vomiting, followed by mild jaundice. Physical examination reveals tender hepatomegaly extending 1.5 cm below the costal margin and transient cutaneous lesions with joint pain. What is the most common extrahepatic feature of this infection?
questions.exp: In HAV, tender hepatomegaly (max 2 cm) is found, and rash/arthralgia is explicitly annotated as the most common '(m/c)' extrahepatic feature. (Book p993)

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: Match each viral hepatitis with its characteristic diagnostic serology — 1) Acute Hepatitis A 2) Acute Hepatitis E … A) Anti-HEV IgM positive, which can persist up to 4 months B) Anti-HAV IgM positive with mixed pattern serum bilirubin elevation
questions.exp: Acute HAV shows Anti-HAV IgM (+) with mixed bilirubin; acute HEV shows Anti-HEV IgM (+) that persists up to 4 months with conjugated bilirubin. (Book p993)

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: Fill up: In acute hepatitis E, the serum bilirubin characteristically exhibits a predominantly ______ pattern accompanied by prominent pruritus.
questions.exp: Under lab investigations for HEV, serum bilirubin is specified as '(conjugated)' and accompanied by cholestatic pruritus. (Book p993)

questions.sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology
questions.q: Which of the following non-viral conditions is NOT listed under 'Others' as a cause of acute hepatitis?
questions.exp: The 'Others' category lists Autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's disease, AFLP, and Budd-Chiari syndrome; hemochromatosis is a cause of chronic liver disease (p989). (Book p993)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: What is the incidence of fulminant hepatic failure in acute Hepatitis A versus acute Hepatitis E in pregnancy?
opts: HAV: rare (1 in 2 lakhs); HEV in pregnancy: approximately 20%
questions.exp: Risk of fulminant failure is rare in HAV (1 in 2 lakhs), whereas in HEV it is 1–2% in general but reaches 20% in pregnancy. (Book p994)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: What are the typical recovery durations for acute Hepatitis A versus acute Hepatitis E infections?
questions.exp: The comparison table notes a recovery time of 8 weeks for HAV and 12 weeks for HEV. (Book p994)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: Match each hepatitis virus with its specific medical therapy — 1) Hepatitis A fluid and glucose repletion 2) Hepatitis E with long-standing cholestasis … A) Oral or systemic steroids B) 150 mL of 10% Dextrose
questions.exp: Conservative glucose repletion for HAV uses 150 mL 10% Dextrose, whereas long-standing cholestasis in HEV is treated with steroids. (Book p994)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: Fill up: Acute relapsing hepatitis occurring > 6–12 months after the initial infection is observed in ______ but is absent in Hepatitis E.
questions.exp: The table notes '+ (Relapse >6–12 months)' under HAV for acute relapsing hepatitis, while HEV has a dash. (Book p994)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: What is the recommended dosing schedule and pre-exposure timing for the HAVRIX Hepatitis A vaccine?
opts: 2 mL IM, 3 doses at 0, 1, 6 months; pre-exposure 6 weeks before travel
1 mL oral drops, 2 doses 4 weeks apart; pre-exposure 1 week before travel
1 mL IM, 2 doses given 6–12 months apart; pre-exposure >= 2 weeks before travel
0.5 mL SC, single dose; pre-exposure within 48 hours of travel
questions.exp: HAVRIX is given as 1 mL IM in 2 doses 6–12 months apart; pre-exposure prophylaxis is >= 2 weeks before travel, and post-exposure within 4 weeks. (Book p994)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: Which three laboratory parameters constitute the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score noted on this page?
opts: ALT, Platelet count, and Serum Sodium
GGT, Alkaline phosphatase, and Encephalopathy grade
INR, Serum Bilirubin, and Serum Creatinine
Albumin, Prothrombin time, and Ascites grade
questions.exp: The MELD score components are explicitly listed as INR, Serum Bilirubin, and Serum Creatinine. (Book p994)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: A traveler returns from an endemic zone with acute viral hepatitis A. Serological plotting over the 20-week exposure window demonstrates stool virus shedding followed by jaundice. At what post-exposure time frame does fecal HAV shedding peak and drop, and which antibody provides lifelong immunity?
opts: Fecal shedding persists continuously for 12 months; IgA Anti-HAV provides lifelong immunity
Fecal shedding only begins after week 16; Anti-HBs provides lifelong immunity
Fecal shedding peaks before 4 weeks and drops by 6 weeks; IgG Anti-HAV provides lifelong immunity
Fecal shedding peaks at 12 weeks and drops at 20 weeks; IgM Anti-HAV provides lifelong immunity
questions.exp: The graph shows fecal HAV peaking before week 4 and dropping by week 6; IgG Anti-HAV rises after weeks 8–12 conferring lifelong protection. (Book p994)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: What is the clinical definition of Acute Liver Failure (ALF)?
opts: Biliary tract obstruction complicated by ascending cholangitis and septic shock
Acute hepatitis with encephalopathy (cerebral edema) and coagulopathy (INR >= 1.5) without pre-existing liver disease
Decompensation of established cirrhosis with ascites, variceal bleeding, and jaundice
Severe transaminitis >1000 U/L persisting for more than 6 months in a chronic carrier
questions.exp: ALF is defined as acute hepatitis plus encephalopathy (cerebral edema) and coagulopathy (INR >= 1.5) in the absence of pre-existing liver disease. (Book p994)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: Match each classification of acute liver failure with its onset interval from jaundice to encephalopathy — 1) Fulminant (Hyperacute) 2) Acute 3) Subacute … A) 7–21 days B) 21 days to 26 weeks C) < 7 days
questions.exp: Onset intervals are Fulminant (Hyperacute): < 7 days; Acute: 7–21 days; and Subacute: 21 days to 26 weeks. (Book p994)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: What is the most common cause of Acute Liver Failure in India?
questions.exp: Under viral causes of ALF, HEV (1–2%) is explicitly tagged as '(m/c in India)'. (Book p994)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: What is the risk of developing acute liver failure in patients with Hepatitis B and Hepatitis D virus coinfection?
questions.exp: The risk of ALF in HBV + HDV coinfection is listed as 5–20% (compared to 0.1–1% for isolated HBV). (Book p994)

questions.sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification
questions.q: Assess the two statements: I Hepatitis E carries no commercial vaccine approved for routine clinical prevention. II Post-exposure prophylaxis for Hepatitis A using HAVRIX vaccine must be administered within 4 weeks of exposure.
questions.exp: Both statements are true: HEV has 'No vaccine' listed, and HAVRIX post-exposure prophylaxis is given 'within 4 wks'. (Book p994)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: Match each etiology of drug-induced acute liver failure with its geographic epidemiology or mechanism — 1) Paracetamol 2) Rifampicin … A) Idiosyncratic dose-independent toxicity that can occur after a single dose B) Most common cause of acute liver failure in Europe
questions.exp: Paracetamol is the most common cause of ALF in Europe ('m/c in Europe'), while Rifampicin is an idiosyncratic reaction that can occur after a single dose. (Book p995)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: What are the maximum daily therapeutic dose and the acute toxic threshold dose for paracetamol (acetaminophen)?
opts: Maximum therapeutic: 1 g/day; Toxic dose: > 5 g/day
Maximum therapeutic: 4 g/day; Toxic dose: > 7.5 g/day
Maximum therapeutic: 2 g/day; Toxic dose: > 4 g/day
Maximum therapeutic: 6 g/day; Toxic dose: > 12 g/day
questions.exp: The book specifies for Paracetamol: max dose 4 g/day and toxic dose > 7.5 g/day. (Book p995)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: Which of the following drugs is NOT listed as causing dose-independent (idiosyncratic) Acute Liver Failure?
questions.exp: Mushroom toxin is listed under dose-dependent causes along with paracetamol; carbamazepine, PTU, valproate, nitrofurantoin, phenytoin, INH, and single-dose rifampicin are idiosyncratic. (Book p995)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: What is the primary pathophysiological driver of hepatic encephalopathy and seizures in acute liver failure?
opts: Elevated intracranial tension and cerebral edema
questions.exp: In ALF, hepatic encephalopathy is due to '↑ ICT & Cerebral edema -> Seizures'. (Book p995)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: Assess the two clinical features of acute liver failure: I Coagulopathy is defined by an INR > 1.5, yet the clinical risk of spontaneous overt bleeding is rare. II Active alcohol consumption decreases overall mortality in acute liver failure.
questions.exp: Statement I is true because coagulopathy has INR > 1.5 but bleeding is rare. Statement II is false because alcohol causes '↑ mortality'. (Book p995)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: Fill up: In paracetamol hepatotoxicity, excessive metabolism by cytochrome ______ in Zone 3 hepatocytes generates the toxic metabolite NAPQI.
questions.exp: Paracetamol is converted to NAPQI by CYP2E1 in Zone 3 hepatocytes. (Book p995)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: Why does NAPQI cause hepatocellular necrosis in paracetamol poisoning?
opts: Glutathione stores are depleted, leaving NAPQI un-metabolized to covalently bind hepatic proteins
NAPQI directly blocks canalicular MRP-2 excretion of bile salts
NAPQI irreversibly uncouples mitochondrial electron transport at Complex I
NAPQI triggers rapid apoptosis of sinusoidal Kupffer cells
questions.exp: Accumulated NAPQI is not metabolized because of depletion in hepatic glutathione stores, leading to hepatotoxicity. (Book p995)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: Match each clinical stage of paracetamol poisoning with its post-ingestion timeline — 1) Stage I 2) Stage II 3) Stage III 4) Stage IV … A) 72–96 hours B) < 24 hours C) > 96 hours D) 24–72 hours
questions.exp: Timeline: Stage I is <24 hr, Stage II is 24–72 hr, Stage III is 72–96 hr, and Stage IV is >96 hr. (Book p995)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 80 hours after ingesting a large handful of acetaminophen tablets. He is in Stage III toxicity. Which laboratory and clinical features characterise this critical stage?
opts: Mild nausea and vomiting with entirely normal transaminases and normal INR
Isolated right upper quadrant tenderness with AST < 100 U/L and absent jaundice
Complete clinical recovery with normalization of all liver enzymes
Hepatic encephalopathy, cerebral edema, bilirubin > 4.5 mg/dL, ATN, hypoglycemia, and lactic acidosis
questions.exp: Stage III (72–96 hrs, which determines survival) features encephalopathy, cerebral edema, coagulopathy, bilirubin > 4.5 mg/dL, ATN, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, lactic acidosis, and MODS. (Book p995)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: Which stage of paracetamol toxicity is explicitly identified as the stage that 'Determines survival'?
questions.exp: Stage III (72–96 hrs) is specifically annotated with '(Determines survival)'. (Book p995)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: Fill up: In Stage III paracetamol toxicity, acute renal failure characteristically arises from ______ complicated by sepsis.
questions.exp: The table lists 'ATN (Acute Tubular Necrosis) : sepsis + renal failure' in Stage III. (Book p995)

questions.sec: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages
questions.q: What serum bilirubin cut-off is listed as a feature of Stage III paracetamol poisoning?
questions.exp: Stage III features explicitly include 'Bilirubin > 4.5 mg/dL'. (Book p995)

questions.sec: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
questions.q: Which graphic assessment tool is used to evaluate the severity of acetaminophen intoxication and determine the need for antidote therapy?
questions.exp: The nomogram is titled 'Rumack Matthew Nomogram: Severity of acetaminophen intoxication'. (Book p996)

questions.sec: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
questions.q: Match each axis of the Rumack-Matthew nomogram with the physiological parameter it plots — 1) X-axis 2) Y-axis … A) Plasma acetaminophen concentration (µg/mL and µmol/L) B) Hours after ingestion (from 0 to 24 hours)
questions.exp: The X-axis plots hours after ingestion (0 to 24), and the Y-axis plots plasma acetaminophen concentration in µg/mL and µmol/L. (Book p996)

questions.sec: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
questions.q: According to King's College Hospital criteria for acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure, what arterial pH cut-off is an independent indicator of poor prognosis?
opts: Arterial pH < 7.35 within 12 hours of ingestion
Arterial pH < 7.10 within 4 hours of ingestion
Arterial pH < 7.25 more than 24 hours after drug ingestion
questions.exp: The first major criterion is 'Arterial pH < 7.25 more than 24 hours after drug ingestion'. (Book p996)

questions.sec: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
questions.q: In the absence of arterial pH < 7.25, which of the following is NOT one of the King's College triad criteria for poor prognosis in acetaminophen ALF?
opts: Serum creatinine level > 3.4 mg/dL (300 µmol/L) or anuria
questions.exp: The three concurrent King's College criteria are PT > 100 s (INR > 6.5), Creatinine > 3.4 mg/dL (300 µmol/L) or anuria, and Grade 3–4 encephalopathy; bilirubin is not part of this triad. (Book p996)

questions.sec: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
questions.q: A patient presents within 4 hours of ingesting a massive acute overdose of paracetamol. What is the initial decontamination procedure indicated before antidote administration?
questions.exp: For presentations < 4 hrs, the first treatment listed is 'Charcoal hemoperfusion'. (Book p996)

questions.sec: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
questions.q: What is the drug of choice (DOC) for paracetamol overdose?
questions.exp: N-acetyl Cysteine (NAC) is designated as 'DOC' for acetaminophen toxicity. (Book p996)

questions.sec: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
questions.q: What post-ingestion deadline is recommended for optimal hepatoprotective efficacy when administering N-acetylcysteine (NAC)?
questions.exp: The protocol states: 'Given within 15 hours'. (Book p996)

questions.sec: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
questions.q: Match each infusion phase of the standard IV N-acetylcysteine protocol with its exact dose and duration — 1) Phase 1 2) Phase 2 3) Phase 3 … A) 100 mg/kg in 1 L of 5% Dextrose over the next 16 hours B) 150 mg/kg in 200 mL of 5% Dextrose over 15–60 minutes C) 50 mg/kg in 500 mL of 5% Dextrose over 4 hours
questions.exp: The 3-stage infusion is: 1) 150 mg/kg in 200 mL 5% Dextrose over 15–60 min; 2) 50 mg/kg in 500 mL 5% Dextrose over 4 hr; 3) 100 mg/kg in 1 L 5% Dextrose over 16 hr. (Book p996)

questions.sec: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
questions.q: Which oral sulfur-containing amino acid is listed as an alternative therapeutic option to N-acetylcysteine in paracetamol toxicity?
questions.exp: Under treatment options, item c lists 'methionine'. (Book p996)

questions.sec: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
questions.q: Assess the two statements on N-acetylcysteine: I N-acetylcysteine is also used therapeutically in non-acetaminophen drug-induced hepatotoxicity. II King's College criteria for poor prognosis in acetaminophen cases require both pH < 7.25 AND Grade 3 encephalopathy to be present together.
questions.exp: Statement I is true because the note states NAC is used in other drug-induced hepatotoxicity. Statement II is false because pH < 7.25 is an independent predictor on its own; alternatively, all three other criteria must be present. (Book p996)

questions.sec: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
questions.q: A 30-year-old woman is admitted 30 hours after an intentional acetaminophen overdose. Her arterial blood gas shows pH 7.21, serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, and INR 3.2. She is drowsy but conversant (Grade 1 encephalopathy). How does she meet the King's College poor prognosis criteria?
opts: She meets the criteria because her INR exceeds 6.5
She meets the criteria because she has Grade 4 coma
She does not meet any poor prognosis criterion
She meets the independent criterion of arterial pH < 7.25 more than 24 hours post-ingestion
questions.exp: Arterial pH < 7.25 after 24 hours alone fulfills the King's College poor prognosis criteria, irrespective of encephalopathy grade or creatinine. (Book p996)

units.title: Acute hepatitis etiologies and HAV versus HEV clinical profiles
units.guide: Acute hepatitis outcomes (recovery m/c), viral causes (HAV in children, HEV in adults), drug and toxin causes (paracetamol, yellow phosphorus, mushrooms), and the complete HAV versus HEV comparison table (Picornaviridae vs Hepeviridae, feco-oral spread, incubation 30 vs 40 days, cytopathic vs immune injury, cholestatic pruritus, and IgM serology).

units.title: HAV vs HEV outcomes, serological kinetics and ALF classification
units.guide: FHF risk (HAV 1 in 2 lakhs vs HEV 20% in pregnancy), 8 vs 12 week recovery, HAVRIX vaccine (2 doses 6-12 months apart), MELD score parameters, the 20-week serological curve with stool shedding and IgM/IgG kinetics, ALF definition (hepatitis + encephalopathy + INR >= 1.5 without prior disease), and hyperacute/acute/subacute onset categories.

units.title: ALF causes, idiosyncratic DILI and Paracetamol stages I–IV
units.guide: Paracetamol m/c in Europe, dose-dependent (>7.5 g/day) vs idiosyncratic drugs (single-dose rifampicin, carbamazepine, PTU), CYP2E1 zone 3 NAPQI generation with glutathione depletion, and the four clinical stages of paracetamol poisoning culminating in Stage III survival-determining failure.

units.title: Rumack-Matthew nomogram, King's College criteria and NAC protocol
units.guide: Rumack-Matthew nomogram risk lines, King's College poor prognosis criteria (pH < 7.25 after 24 hr OR triad of PT > 100 s / INR > 6.5, creatinine > 3.4 mg/dL / anuria, and grade 3-4 encephalopathy), charcoal hemoperfusion < 4 hr, three-bag IV N-acetylcysteine infusion protocol, and oral methionine.
